text: A logical circuit diagram doesn't know or care which physical qubits anything runs on — it just draws a gate between two wires. Real hardware isn't that forgiving, and the gap between the two is where a compiler's hardest work, and a real chunk of a circuit's final error, actually comes from.

When you write a circuit, a two-qubit gate between qubit 3 and qubit 7 is just a line connecting two wires — nothing encodes whether they're anywhere near each other on real hardware. Before a circuit can run, a compiler step called transpilation or routing maps each logical qubit onto a specific physical qubit, then rewrites any gate that falls outside the device's connectivity graph into something the hardware can actually execute. The standard way to do that is the SWAP detour: insert SWAP gates that physically move one qubit's state, one hop at a time, until the two qubits that need to interact are adjacent.

Here's a concrete, verified example. Say a circuit needs a gate between two qubits sitting at graph distance 3 apart. Bringing them adjacent takes 2 SWAPs — one fewer than the distance, since the last hop is where the real gate happens. On superconducting hardware, each SWAP is typically built from 3 CNOTs, so those 2 SWAPs cost 6 CNOTs, plus the 1 CNOT for the actual gate — 7 total two-qubit operations where the logical circuit asked for 1. At a representative 0.5 percent error rate per gate, the direct version carries about a 0.5 percent error chance; the routed version, with 7 total operations, carries closer to 3.4 percent — nearly seven times higher, purely from routing.

Every real device has only so much usable circuit depth before accumulated error overwhelms the result. Routing overhead spends part of that limited budget on gates that don't advance the computation at all — they only exist to work around the chip's wiring. A circuit that looks like it needs 40 native two-qubit gates can end up executing well over 60 after routing, depending on how badly its logical connectivity pattern mismatches the device's physical graph.

Next lesson goes one level deeper: what a SWAP actually costs in real gates, how compilers try to minimize that cost across an entire circuit, and why routing overhead can end up dominating the total error budget on large or deep circuits.
